title: Neural Data as Property: Who Owns Your Thoughts
body:
The legal status of neural interface data in Meridian 88 is governed by a patchwork of three overlapping frameworks: the Corponation Intellectual Assets Doctrine of 2163, the Meridian Personal Data Sovereignty Charter of 2179, and the Federal Cognitive Privacy Act of 2181 — which applies nominally to the megacity but is widely understood to be unenforceable within Corporate Zones. The result is that the ownership of data generated by a person's own brain depends almost entirely on which geographic zone they were in when the data was recorded, which hardware manufacturer produced their interface, and whether they signed an end-user agreement at any point in the preceding seven years. Most people have signed dozens of such agreements embedded in firmware update prompts.

The Corponation Intellectual Assets Doctrine established the principle of 'generative attribution,' which holds that data produced while using a corponation's infrastructure — including its licensed BCI network frequencies — is a co-generated asset subject to a default 60/40 split favoring the corponation. This doctrine was challenged in the landmark 2184 case Delacroix v. Vantara Neural Systems, in which plaintiff Seun Delacroix argued that memories recorded during her off-hours commute were being sold to a predictive retail consortium without her knowledge. The Meridian Arbitration Chamber ruled in Vantara's favor on the grounds that her transit pass constituted a network access agreement and that 'ambient cognitive residue' fell within the generative attribution framework. The ruling is now cited in approximately 800 cases per year.

The Personal Data Sovereignty Charter was a citizen-assembly initiative that succeeded in establishing a formal 'cognitive commons' classification for certain categories of neural data: raw emotional valence readings, sleep-state recordings, and data generated during declared medical events. Under the Charter, this data cannot be commercially licensed without explicit tiered consent — a process managed through the Meridian Data Registry, a municipal database that is perpetually underfunded and runs on infrastructure last meaningfully upgraded in 2191. The Registry's backlog of consent dispute filings currently exceeds 400,000 cases, with an average resolution time of 31 months.

In practice, most Meridian residents operate under what legal scholars at the Calumet Institute of Policy call 'functional data destitution' — a condition in which an individual technically retains rights to their neural data but lacks the legal resources, standing, or procedural access to exercise those rights. Corporate-tier citizens have access to Neural Rights Advocates, a specialized legal subprofession, through their employment packages. Registered-tier citizens can access a limited pool of pro-bono Neural Rights Clinics, the largest of which — the Wicker Park Cognitive Commons Clinic — handles roughly 2,000 cases per year against a citywide need estimated at over 200,000. Below Registered tier, neural data rights are effectively theoretical.
headings: The Personal Data Sovereignty Charter and Its Limits
